translation: Two other small, scallop-edged photos, probably from the same year, show the same child, but smaller in frilly dresses and puffed sleeves.
In the first one, she impishly nestles up against a woman with a massive body engulfed in a broad-striped dress, her hair bundled up into hefty swirls.
In the other, she raises her left fist; her right one is being held by a tall man in a light jacket and pleated pants who appears nonchalant.
Both photos were taken on the same day against a short wall topped with border plants in a paved courtyard.
Above their heads is a clothesline where one clothespin still clings on.

Another photo, signed by the same photographer but on more ordinary paper and without the gold border probably intended for the same family distribution shows a little girl of about four, solemn, almost sad despite her chubby-cheeked good looks beneath short hair parted in the middle and pulled back with clips to which ribbons are attached like butterflies.
Her left hand rests on the same carved table, now fully visible and in a Louis XVI style.
She appears plump in her blouse; her pinafore skirt is riding up at the front because of a prominent stomach, perhaps indicative of rickets (circa 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment, and everyone thought they looked grand in their uniforms.
On the evening of their enlistment, they did rounds in the cafes to celebrate their acknowledgement as real men.
Before joining the army, they were still children who had little worth on the job market or in marriage.
Afterward, they could have a wife and children.
Their uniforms, paraded around the neighborhood during leave, wrapped them up in patriotic beauty and potential sacrifice.
The shadow of victorious warriors––of GIs—hovered around them.
The rough fabric of their jackets touched when you stood on your tiptoes to kiss them symbolized a distinct divide between male and female worlds.
Seeing them inspired feelings of heroism.

Beneath the unchanging surface, last year's circus posters with a photo of Roger Lanzac, first communion pictures handed out to friends, the Club des Chansonniers on Radio Luxembourg, days were filled with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, one would press against the window of the general electricity store to watch television.
Cafes invested in buying a set to attract customers.
Motocross trails snaked up and down hillsides and we would watch vehicles ascend and descend all day long amidst an ear-splitting din.
The growing impatience of commerce shaking up small-town life with its new buzzwords: "initiative," "dynamism.
Between carnivals and festivals, commercial fortnights established themselves as springtime rites.
In downtown streets loudspeakers blared encouragements to buy interspersed with songs by Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine while offering chances to win a Simca or dining room suite.
On stage in front of City Hall a local host told jokes from Roger Nicolas and Jean Richard repertoire, drummed up contestants for Quiz shows just like on radio broadcasts.
Sitting at one corner of the stage under her crown was the Queen of Commerce reigning supreme over proceedings.
Goods were paraded in festive colors; people would comment "how different things are" or "one mustn't stagnate; it is dulling staying at home all day.
But they only talked about what they had seen, which could be relived by eating and drinking.
They did not have enough talent or conviction to talk about what they knew but had not seen.
So neither of Jewish children boarding trains for Auschwitz, nor of the starving dead picked up in the Warsaw Ghetto in the morning, nor of the 10,000 degrees at Hiroshima.

Hence this impression that history classes, documentaries and films later would not dispel: neither the crematory ovens nor the atomic bomb were in the same era as black-market butter, air raid warnings and trips to  basement shelters.
They spoke metaphorically about the previous war, the Great one, that of '14, won in blood and glory, a man's war that the women at the table listened to with respect.
They talked about Chemin des Dames and Verdun, about those gassed, and about hearing the bells on November 11th 1918.
They named villages from which not a single child who had gone to the front had returned.
They contrasted soldiers in muddied trenches with prisoners from '40; warm and sheltered for five years without even experiencing bombs falling over their heads.
They argued over who owned heroism and misfortune.

The children were not listening and were quick to leave the table as soon as they had permission, taking advantage of the general goodwill on festive days to engage in forbidden games, bouncing on the beds and swinging upside down.
But they absorbed everything.

Next to the fabulous time of which they would not arrange episodes for a long while the Debacle, The Exodus, The Occupation, The Landing, The Victory seemed duller than their unnamed present where they were growing up.
They regretted not having been born or barely being when one had to depart in cohorts down roads and sleep on straw like gypsies.
Of this un-lived time, they would harbor a stubborn regret.
Others' memory passed onto them a secret nostalgia for this era that was just missed out on; and hope that one day it will be lived through.
The frenzy that had followed the Liberation was fading.
People only thought about going out and the world was full of desires to be satisfied immediately.
Everything that constituted a first time since the war sparked a rush: bananas, National Lottery tickets, fireworks.

Whole neighborhoods, from grandmothers supported by their daughters to infants in prams, threw themselves at the fair, torchlight retreats, Bouglione Circus where they risked being trampled in the scramble.
As a prayerful and singing crowd they would take to the road to welcome Our Lady of Boulogne's statue and accompany her for miles on end on her way back.
Secular or religious gatherings were all good excuses for them to be outside together as though they wanted to continue living collectively.

On Sunday evenings busloads wouldn't return from sea without large young men in shorts yelling songs while perched on top of luggage racks; dogs roamed freely and were mating right there in broad daylight street.
Family narrative and social narrative are one and the same.

The voices of the guests outlined the territories of youth: the countryside and farms where, in time long forgotten, men were appointed and girls served; the factory where they all met, got to know each other and married, small businesses to which those with ambition ascended.
Their stories were without personal events except births, marriages or deaths.
There were no trips outside of their regiment in a distant garrison town; their lives filled with work, its toughness and exhaustion or threats from drink.
School was a mythical backdrop a brief golden age with its strict godlike teacher ruling over it with his iron rod used for striking on fingers.
Brown pictures passed from hand to hand, their backs stained by every finger that had held them during other meals—a mix of coffee and grease melded into an indescribable colour.
In the stiff and solemn couples, the wedding guests lined up on several rows along a wall, one didn't recognise either their parents or anyone else.
It was not oneself either that was seen in the half-naked baby of indistinct gender lying on a cushion but someone else—a creature belonging to a mute and inaccessible time.
